work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Stimulating other nodes can break pharmacoresistance in many pathway models
statement: In 17 of the 27 habituating BioModels pathway models (about 63%), stimulating a third node (neither the stimulus nor the response) abolished habituation for some stimulus–response pairs, so some biological networks contain discoverable stimulus nodes that may serve to break pharmacoresistance without rewiring the network.
quote: Overall, we conclude that in some biological networks, there are discoverable stimulus nodes that may serve towards breaking pharmacoresistance.
scope: 27 habituating ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Sensitization is common in biological pathway models but rare in random networks
statement: Sensitization (a progressive 1.5-fold increase in response over repeated stimulations) was found in 27 of the 35 BioModels pathway models, whereas very few random gene-circuit models showed it (under 10% of pairings per model), suggesting the feature may be unique to biology or require more complex random models.
quote: Interestingly, very few of the random models had UCS-R relations that generated sensitization (<10% of UCS-R pairings per model), indicating that this feature may be unique to biology, or that more complex random models would be needed to find such behavior (Figure 10 and Figures S17–S19).
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus 500 random gene-circuit models

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Sensitization is harder to break than habituation in pathway models
statement: In ODE pathway models, sensitization could be broken by stimulating a third node in only 8 of 27 sensitizing models, mostly for fewer than 5% of node pairs, so breaking sensitization is less likely than breaking habituation and therapies may need other avenues of intervention.
quote: Overall, we conclude that while sensitization is prevalent in biological models, the breaking of sensitization is less likely than in habituation, and therefore therapeutic models may need to pursue other avenues of intervention.
scope: 27 sensitizing ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Standard topology measures are likely insufficient to design or evolve memory
statement: Because random networks matched to biological pathway models in number of nodes, edges, indegree, outdegree, betweenness, PageRank and hubness lack comparable memory, those structural features are not likely to be sufficient criteria for designing or evolving networks with memories.
quote: Interestingly, since the random networks were designed to match the biological models in number of nodes, number of edges, indegree, outdegree, betweenness, PageRank, and hubness, those features are not likely to be sufficient criteria for designing (or evolving) networks with memories.
scope: Gene regulatory and protein pathway networks

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Oscillatory pathway networks may gain more memory from noise
statement: Biswas, Clawson and Levin hypothesize that biological networks with strong oscillatory components (such as cell-cycle, circadian-clock and developmental-timer models) may benefit more from noise in terms of memory, analogous to harmonic resonance, though some oscillatory models did not show this.
quote: From this, we hypothesize that biological networks with strong oscillatory components may benefit more, from a memory perspective, to noise, similar to the case of harmonic resonance [122].
scope: ODE models of oscillatory biological networks (cell cycle, circadian clocks, developmental timers)

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pathway memory is more robust to edge perturbation, perhaps from selection
statement: The memory capacity of biological ODE pathway models degrades significantly less than that of random networks when edges are randomly deleted and added, perhaps because of evolutionary pressure to handle changing environments.
quote: The memory capability of biological models is also much more robust to edge perturbation than those of random networks, as indicated in Figure 7, perhaps due to evolutionary pressure to handle changing environments.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus random gene-circuit models

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pulsatile signalling may let cells behaviour-shape each other in vivo
statement: Because transcriptional and other signalling mechanisms are pulsatile, cells may apply timed behaviour-shaping stimuli to each other in vivo, exploiting the trainability of their pathways to evolve complex phenotypes, though the role of trainability in evolution and development is unknown.
quote: The role of trainability in evolution and development is as yet unknown, but it is interesting that transcriptional [126] and other [127,128] biological signaling mechanisms are now seen as pulsatile, which affords rich opportunity for cells to apply timed “behavior shaping” stimuli to each other in vivo, as a way of exploiting the multiscale competency of biological material to evolve complex phenotypes [129].
scope: Cells and tissues in vivo

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Developmental physiology is the control layer between genotype and phenotype
statement: The authors hold that biological genotypes do not code directly for phenotypes; developmental physiology, built from cells with their own context-sensitive behaviours, is the control layer separating genomes from the capacities that selection evaluates.
quote: Biological genotypes do not code directly for phenotypes; developmental physiology is the control layer that separates genomes from capacities ascertained by selection.
scope: Multicellular organisms generally

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Planaria combine a messy mixoploid genome with highly reliable anatomy
statement: Because planaria reproduce by fission and regeneration and so retain somatic mutations, they have a very messy, mixoploid genome, yet they have highly reliable anatomy, with every fragment regenerating a normal worm.
quote: As a result, planaria have an incredibly messy genome (indeed, worms are mixoploid—different numbers of chromosomes in each cell). Despite this, they have the most reliable anatomy: every fragment of a planarian regenerates a perfect worm each time.
scope: Asexual, fissiparous planarians (e.g. Schmidtea mediterranea asexual strain)

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Cellular competencies come by default, unlike organism-level learning
statement: Unlike organism-level learning, which requires mechanisms such as nervous systems that must themselves be evolved and paid for, cellular competencies come by default because cells already carry capabilities evolved when their ancestors were independent organisms.
quote: In contrast, cellular competencies come “by default” because organisms consist of cellular components that already have many capabilities evolved during their ancestral lifetime as independent organisms.
scope: Cells of multicellular organisms and their unicellular ancestors

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Higher cellular competency accelerates evolutionary search in a 1D embryo model
statement: In a minimal artificial embryogeny model (1D integer arrays whose fitness is their monotonicity, with competent cells performing a restricted bubble sort before fitness evaluation), populations with higher cellular competency reached high fitness faster and more consistently than hardwired populations, e.g. under 6 generations at competency 400 versus over 200 for hardwired.
quote: These data demonstrate the role competency plays in non-linearly improving the rate of fitness of a population and support a clear conclusion: the higher the competency, the better the performance.
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos evolved with a genetic algorithm

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Cellular competency reduces selective pressure on structural genes
statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model, the genotypic fitness of competent populations rose briefly and then plateaued below that of hardwired populations, with wider variance at higher competency, showing that competency delivers high phenotypic fitness but reduces selective pressure on the structural genes.
quote: Thus, as hypothesized, increasing competency in our simulation enabled excellent performance but reduced selective pressure on the embryo’s structural genes.
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos evolved with a genetic algorithm

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Competent embryos take over mixed populations given enough competency or numbers
statement: In mixed populations of the 1D artificial embryogeny model, competent embryos starting as a minority came to dominate hardwired ones within two or three generations, and the competency needed to dominate fell as their initial share rose (75 at 10%, 40 at 20%, 10 at 30%), while at 2.5% they did not dominate even at competency 95.
quote: As their initial proportion in the population increased, competent embryos required progressively less competency to dominate over their hardwired competitors.
scope: In silico mixed populations of 200 hardwired and competent 1D embryos

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Evolvable competency rises rapidly and plateaus at a high level
statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model, when competency is set by an evolvable gene (range 1–500, initialized at 1–15), the best individual's competency rose rapidly and plateaued around 470, higher than the roughly 364 needed for maximum fitness, a level the authors attribute to random drift among equally fit values.
quote: The prevalence of the competency allele rapidly rose, meandering and exploring values up to 485 during evolution (shaded area in Figure 5A) before plateauing at ~470.
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos with an evolvable competency gene over 1000 generations

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Evolvable competency decouples genotypic from phenotypic fitness
statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model with evolvable competency, the correlation between genotypic and phenotypic fitness fell to zero within about 20 generations, so allowing competency to evolve disrupts selection's ability to pick the best structural genes.
quote: Correlation dropped to 0 within about 20 generations as individuals who succeeded because of their developmental competencies rapidly dominated the population. We conclude that allowing competency to evolve disrupts the ability to select for the best structural genes.
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos with an evolvable competency gene

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: A cost on competency restores a Baldwin effect and genetic assimilation
statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model, penalizing fitness in proportion to competency (penalty factors 1×10⁻⁷ to 0.5) produced a Baldwin effect: structural-gene fitness kept improving, selection favoured progressively lower competency, and early competency-based gains were assimilated into the structural genes; the authors note real competency costs are unmeasured.
quote: Thus early gains based on the competency gene are later assimilated into the structural genes, paralleling what has been described previously in the context of organism-level learning [59].
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos with a fitness penalty on competency

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Planaria are an example of runaway cellular competency
statement: The authors propose that planaria exemplify runaway competency: their cells became so good at compensating for structural-gene deficiencies that selection could no longer pick the best genomes, so evolution instead increased generic competency to reach the target morphology, explaining a chaotic genome with robust anatomy.
quote: We propose that planaria are an example of runaway competency: when cells get really good at making up for deficiencies in the structural genes, evolution has such a hard time selecting for the best genomes that further improvements instead increase generic competency to reach their target morphology despite perturbations.
scope: Planarian flatworms

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Planaria lack morphological mutant lines; the only abnormal line is bioelectric
statement: Unlike other model species, planaria have no reported morphologically abnormal genetic strains; the only abnormal line is a permanently two-headed form produced by manipulating bioelectric signalling rather than genes, which the authors say is predicted by their model for species like planaria.
quote: In planaria this does not exist—no morphologically abnormal genetic strains have been reported. In fact, the only available abnormal line of planaria is a permanently two-headed form [96,97,98], which was produced not genetically but by manipulating bioelectrical signaling—the modality that is used to coordinate cellular competency [99,100,101], as is predicted by our model for species like planaria.
scope: Planarian flatworms compared with other model organisms

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Evolution changes the competency gene more often than any structural gene
statement: In the 1D artificial embryogeny model with evolvable competency, positional changes to cells over 1000 generations resulted from changes to the competency gene significantly more often than from changes to any of the fifty structural genes.
quote: We found that the competency gene is changed significantly more often over the course of evolution than any structural gene (Figure 6).
scope: In silico 1D artificial embryos with an evolvable competency gene

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: An intelligence ratchet locks evolution into improving cellular competency
statement: The authors suggest that because competency hides genetic deficiencies from selection, a positive-feedback ratchet arises in which evolution increasingly improves the problem-solving competency (intelligence) of its cellular material rather than the structural genome, a possible driver for scaling intelligence in morphological and other spaces.
quote: This suggests the existence of a powerful ratchet mechanism in which evolution progressively becomes locked into improvements in the intelligence of the agential material with which it works, with reduced pressure on the structural genes.
scope: Evolution of developmental systems; inferred from the 1D artificial embryogeny model

work: Cellular Competency during Development Alters Evolutionary Dynamics in an Artificial Embryogeny Model
label: Problem-solving competency drove evolution long before brains
statement: The authors suggest that intelligence, understood as problem-solving competency, was an evolutionary driver long before complex brains and muscle-driven behaviour arose, so basal cognition is an important part of evolutionary developmental biology.
quote: and that intelligence (problem-solving competency) was an evolutionary driver long before complex brains and muscle-driven behavior arose [52,53,56,136,137,138,139,140,141,142,143].
scope: Evolution of life before nervous systems

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolution scales cell-level metabolic homeostasis into a tissue-level French flag axis
statement: In a 2D neural cellular automaton in which each cell only pursues metabolic (energy) homeostasis and is rewarded according to how well its stripe matches the pattern, evolution (ES-HyperNEAT) produced cell collectives with tissue-level setpoints that solve the French flag problem, i.e. organize a body-wide three-valued positional information axis.
quote: Our system showed the evolution of the much more complex setpoints of cell collectives (tissues) that solve a problem in morphospace: the organization of a body-wide positional information axis (the classic French flag problem in developmental biology).
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata with gap-junction signalling, evolved with ES-HyperNEAT

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Robust patterning works best from a homogeneous starting state
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, French flag patterning works less well from random initial cell states, suggesting that robust development is optimized when cells start from a homogeneous undifferentiated baseline, as real embryos do.
quote: It seems to work less well with random initializations, suggesting that robust development is optimized when cells start with a muted, homogeneous ‘baseline’ state, not highly diverse starting states, which is indeed what is observed in real development
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem; analogy to embryos

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolved tissues repair perturbed patterns although repair was never selected for
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, tissues selected only to self-organize the French flag within 100 steps could restore the target pattern after perturbations applied later (e.g. converting two columns of the red stripe to white at step 110), although they failed after very large perturbations such as converting the whole red stripe.
quote: Thus, we conclude that even though we did not specifically reward for anything other than the single self-organizing property, the cells were able to repair to the target setpoint from multiple starting configurations.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Stress spikes precede spontaneous late remodelling in the simulated tissue
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, the tissue spontaneously remodels long after its pattern has stabilized, without external perturbation, and a sharp spike in stress immediately precedes each onset of morphogenetic activity, suggesting that stress drives the morphogenetic changes.
quote: In our simulations, a dramatic spike in stress immediately precedes the sharp onset of extensive morphogenetic activity (see electronic supplementary material, figure S1a), suggesting that stress drives the morphogenetic changes in the tissue.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Long-term tissue stability emerges without selection for it
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, tissues evolved only over 100-step development maintained their pattern for 1000 steps (allostasis), showing that in this model long-term stable survival need not be selected for because intrinsic dynamics and emergent regenerative capacity maintain order in an adult phase.
quote: Thus, we conclude that long-term stable survival does not need to be specifically selected for, as intrinsic dynamics and emergent anatomical regenerative capacity are enough to maintain order through an adult phase.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Blocking stress signalling prevents anatomical homeostasis in a stress-using tissue
statement: In an evolved neural cellular automaton tissue that uses stress as an instructive signal, forcing stress to zero throughout life (a simulated anxiolytic) lowered pattern accuracy (82.8% vs 95.1% at step 90) and killed the red-stripe cells, so anatomical homeostasis was neither reached nor maintained.
quote: These experiments reveal that, in the absence of stress, anatomical homeostasis is not reached nor maintained during the lifetime of the cells.
scope: One evolved tissue in the 2D neural cellular automaton model that uses stress instructively

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolved stress signalling is instructive only at specific concentrations
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, imposing very high stress on an already patterned tissue had no immediate effect on cell states but later altered them, indicating that evolution used stress as a communication code in which stress affects cell behaviour only at specific concentrations.
quote: We conclude that evolution used stress as a communication system using a particular encoding, in which stress level is instructive and has effects on cell behaviour only at specific concentrations.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Stress propagation is not required for patterning but improves adaptation to change
statement: Across 10 evolved neural cellular automaton tissues, stress signalling was not required to solve the French flag problem (only 1 of 10 died without it), but the tissue that used stress instructively scored significantly better when the target morphology was changed mid-development (p = 0.0312), suggesting that spatial propagation of stress information increases adaptive fitness under perturbation.
quote: For this problem, anatomical homeostasis without stress is possible but exploiting spatial propagation of stress information seems to increase adaptive fitness by improving performance in scenarios where the normal process of morphogenesis is impacted by external perturbations.
scope: Ten evolved tissues in the 2D neural cellular automaton model

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolved stress signalling acts paracrine rather than autocrine
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, transfer entropy from a cell's stress to its neighbours' states is much larger than to its own state, suggesting that the key signalling mode of stress is paracrine, not autocrine.
quote: We also compared the transfer entropy from stress of one cell to its own state and found it to be much less important than the transfer entropy from the stress of one cell to the states of its neighbours (figure 8c). This suggests the key signalling mode for the stress is paracrine, not autocrine.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Simulated embryonic regions take turns acting as the organizer
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, transfer entropy between stripes first flows mainly from the red to the white stripe and then reverses, suggesting that the 'organizer' region (a group of cells that instructively patterns others) changes over time and embryonic regions take turns driving large-scale patterning.
quote: The ‘organizer’ region (here defined as a region or group of cells in a tissue that can induce and instructively pattern other cells) seemed to change over time, suggesting embryonic regions take turns driving the large-scale process.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Information flows first from the anatomical loop to single-cell energy
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, transfer entropy from energy to cell state peaks before the reverse flow, indicating that information is first driven by the tissue-level anatomical homeostatic loop, which then controls the energy cells need to survive; the authors take this to suggest top-down information is key to manipulating tissue dynamics.
quote: Thus, in our scheme, the information was first driven by the anatomical loop, and the energy needed for single-cell survival was controlled by this loop.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Stress rises when cellular memory fails to predict the future
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, stress increases concurrently with a fall in local active information storage of cell states, so evolution used the stress system as a communication channel activated when memory of past events does not predict the future, matching the definition of stressors as unpredictable or uncontrollable stimuli.
quote: In our scheme, evolution used the stress system as a communication system that was activated when memory of past events was not effective for predicting the future.
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Model predicts sudden late remodelling of apparently stable biological patterns
statement: Because the neural cellular automaton suddenly remodelled cell fates after a long period of quiescent, stable pattern, the authors predict that something similar may occur in biological systems: some phenotypes that appear complete may need to be followed much longer to see their true dynamics.
quote: The sudden remodelling of cell fates after a long period of apparently quiescent, stable pattern in our model (figure 4) predicts that something similar may occur in biological systems.
scope: Regenerating and developing organisms, tested in planaria

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: 22% of headless ERK-inhibited planaria spontaneously repattern weeks later
statement: In Dugesia japonica made headless by transient U0126 (ERK/MAP kinase inhibitor) treatment after amputation, 22% of 181 animals followed until death showed sudden repatterning after four or more weeks without any intervention, mostly between 4 and 10 weeks, and 61% of those regained a normal single-headed morphology.
quote: In headless animals observed from when they were cut until their death (n = 181), 22% showed some form of sudden repatterning even though regeneration had completed and morphogenesis had ceased weeks prior (figure 10b).
scope: Dugesia japonica pre-tail fragments treated with 18 μM U0126 for 3 days

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Planarian tissues have processes operating far slower than known regeneration
statement: The spontaneous restoration of normal morphology in headless planaria many weeks after regeneration has completed suggests that planarian tissues contain processes operating on a time scale much longer than previously known.
quote: This spontaneous repatterning that allows the re-establishment of a normal morphology many weeks after regeneration is completed suggests the existence of tissue processes that operate on a time scale much longer than previously known.
scope: Planarian flatworms (Dugesia japonica) after ERK inhibition

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolved tissues show delayed gratification as an unselected free lunch
statement: In the evolved neural cellular automaton, the tissue temporarily moves away from its target pattern to remove misplaced cells and then returns (delayed gratification in the TAME framework), and since neither this nor long-term maintenance was selected for, such capabilities of multi-scale homeostatic systems can emerge as a 'free lunch' without direct selection.
quote: Interestingly, neither of these things were directly selected for during the evolutionary cycle, revealing how some capabilities of multi-scale homeostatic systems can emerge as a kind of ‘free lunch’, without direct selection pressure [2,88].
scope: In silico 2D neural cellular automata evolved for the French flag problem; multi-scale homeostatic systems

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Regeneration can start without injury, so a missing-tissue response may be unnecessary
statement: Because headless planaria mounted a regenerative response with no triggering injury, the authors argue this is consistent with the idea that a missing-tissue response may not be necessary for regeneration and that subtle internal dynamics may suffice to initiate change long after a process seems to have stabilized.
quote: The newly demonstrated ability to mount a regenerative response without any triggering injury is consistent with the idea that a MTR may not be necessary for regeneration to occur [90] and that subtle internal dynamics may be sufficient to initiate change long after the process appears to have reached a stable point.
scope: Planarian regeneration (Dugesia japonica)

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Stress-driven spatial patterning may be conserved across bacteria, metazoa and models
statement: Noting that oscillatory nitrogen stress responses pattern bacterial biofilms and that stress responses define stripe regions in their simulated tissue, the authors suggest that conserved stress-based dynamics could underlie the scaling of spatial patterning from single-cell metabolic goals in bacteria, metazoans and minimal in silico models, similar to the clock-and-wavefront model of somitogenesis.
quote: Thus, conserved dynamics could be relevant across bacterial, metazoan and in silico minimal models of the scaling of spatial patterning from single-cell metabolic and stress dynamics.
scope: Bacterial biofilms, metazoan segmentation, in silico tissue models

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Somatic cells kept their cognitive repertoire and scaled it to anatomical goals
statement: The authors argue that somatic cells did not lose their ancestral cognitive and computational capabilities when they became part of multicellular bodies, but scaled them up to pursue larger anatomical goals.
quote: But somatic cells did not lose their cognitive repertoire and computational capabilities during their transitions to multicellularity or in becoming part of metazoan swarms (bodies): they scaled them to pursue larger anatomical goals [4].
scope: Metazoan somatic cells and their unicellular ancestors

work: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis
label: Evolution pivoted cellular collective intelligence into behavioural intelligence
statement: The authors propose that evolution turned the collective intelligence of cells during body morphogenesis into traditional behavioural intelligence by scaling up the goals (homeostatic setpoints) at the centre of homeostatic processes, so that body patterning and cognition lie on one continuum.
quote: We propose that evolution pivoted the collective intelligence of cells during morphogenesis of the body into traditional behavioural intelligence by scaling up the goals at the centre of homeostatic processes.
scope: Multicellular organisms generally; evolution of morphogenesis and behaviour

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Irreversibility of morphogenesis, not Weismann's barrier, is what limits Lamarckism
statement: Because morphogenesis is a recursive, highly emergent process, the inverse problem of determining which genomic changes would produce a desired large-scale anatomical feature is in general unsolvable, and this irreversibility, rather than any inability to edit the germline in light of somatic experience, is what limits full-scale Lamarckian inheritance.
quote: This irreversibility of the recursive, highly emergent process of morphogenesis is what limits full-scale Lamarckism: the difficulty is not how to penetrate Weismann’s barrier and edit the genome in light of somatic experience—mechanisms exist for this [21–23].
scope: Metazoan development and inheritance in general

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Evolution searches the space of behaviour-shaping signals rather than local rules
statement: Because metazoan cells are agential (they retain adaptive behaviours from unicellular ancestors), what evolution mainly searches is not the enormous space of all possible local rules but the space of behaviour-shaping signals by which cells hack each other's functionality, and the collective intelligence of cell swarms strongly affects the rate and course of evolution.
quote: I argue that what evolution is really searching is not the enormous space of all possible local rules, but instead the space of behavior-shaping signals by which cells hack each other’s functionality, and that the collective intelligence [38, 39] of cellular swarms has major implications for the rate and course of evolution.
scope: Evolution of metazoan anatomy

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: A generative, compressed genome pushes evolution toward general-purpose problem solvers
statement: By using an architecture akin to a variational autoencoder, in which the genome is a compressed generative representation decoded by the developmental layer, evolution is kept from over-training on past conditions and is pushed to produce general-purpose problem-solving organisms that display robustness, plasticity and adaptive success in entirely novel circumstances.
quote: Second is that by using a variational autoencoder-like architecture of compression into a generative genome (Fig. 1), evolution is freed from over-training on past conditions and pushed to evolve general-purpose problem-solving machines which inevitably display robustness, plasticity, and adaptive success in entirely novel circumstances.
scope: Evolution of multicellular organisms

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Gap-junction coupling scales cell competencies into larger collective goal states
statement: Basal cellular competencies were not lost in the transition to multicellularity but scaled up into collective intelligence; gap-junctional merging of intracellular milieus and other tissue-level signalling (e.g. stress propagation) share chemical engrams, erase the individuality of cells, and enlarge the memory, predictive capacity and sensory/effector radius of cell networks so they can pursue larger goal states such as anatomical targets.
quote: This promotes sharing of chemical engrams, which also help to wipe the individuality of cells, and enlarges the memory, predictive capacity, and sensory/effector radius of cellular networks, enabling them to pursue larger goal states in spaces like anatomical morphospace [14].
scope: Multicellular tissues coupled by gap junctions

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Freed from embryonic signals, frog skin cells form self-motile Xenobots
statement: Frog (Xenopus) embryonic epithelial cells, which in vivo form a passive protective outer layer, instead form Xenobots (functional, self-motile constructs with novel behaviours) when liberated from the instructive influences of other cells, showing that such behaviours are normally suppressed by signalling from neighbouring cells during development.
quote: However, when liberated from the instructive influences of the other cells, frog epithelial cells instead form a Xenobot—a functional, self-motile construct with many novel behaviors that are normally suppressed and hidden by the instructive signaling of other cells during development [125].
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic ectoderm explants

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Bioelectric networks were exploited for information integration since bacterial biofilms
statement: Evolution discovered very early, around the time of bacterial biofilms, that electrical networks of ion channels and pumps are a convenient way to integrate and process information across space and time and to scale the functions of individual cells toward large-scale tasks, the same reason brains use this modality.
quote: But evolution discovered very early on, around the time of bacterial biofilms [144], that electric networks are also extremely convenient ways to integrate and process information across space and time, and to scale the functions of individual computing units towards a large-scale task (the same reason that brains, and computers, use this modality [145]).
scope: Bacteria through metazoans

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Reproducing face bioelectric patterns via ion-channel misexpression induces ectopic eyes
statement: The vertebrate face is patterned by bioelectric gradients that regionalize gene expression, and reproducing these voltage patterns elsewhere in a tadpole by misexpressing specific ion channels induces whole ectopic organs such as eyes on the gut or tail, regions not otherwise competent to make eyes in response to Pax6.
quote: Reproducing these patterns elsewhere in the body via misexpression of specific ion channels enables the induction of whole ectopic organs, such as eyes [152] on the gut or tail of a tadpole (thus unlocking novel capabilities of body regions, since only the anterior neurectoderm is competent to make eyes via signals from the chemical master regulator Pax6).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos and tadpoles

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Tadpoles see through an ectopic tail eye without generations of adaptation
statement: Tadpoles whose native eyes are prevented from forming and which carry an ectopic eye on the tail can see and perform well in visual behavioural training even though that eye connects to the spinal cord or peripheral tissue rather than the brain, so a radical change to sensory–motor architecture yields successful behaviour without generations of adaptation.
quote: Tadpoles, in which the native eyes are prevented from forming and an ectopic eye is instead placed on the tail, can see and perform well in visual behavioral training [176], even though the ectopic eye connects to the spinal cord (or just to peripheral tissue) rather than to the brain—this radical change to the sensory–motor architecture does not require generations of adaptation to produce successful behavior.
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eye grafts

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Polyploid newt kidney tubules are built by one giant cell instead of eight to ten
statement: In polyploid newts, whose cells are enlarged by extra genome copies, kidney tubules normally made by eight to ten communicating cells are instead formed by a single enormous cell wrapping around itself, so a different molecular mechanism (cytoskeletal bending rather than cell–cell communication) is deployed to reach the same anatomical outcome, an instance of downward causation in the service of a large-scale anatomical goal.
quote: In the kidney system of polyploid newts, the normal cell:cell communication that creates a tubule from eight to ten cells working together is swapped for a single enormous cell that wraps around itself to create the same final outcome [184].
scope: Polyploid newt pronephric/kidney tubules

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Bioelectric patterns act as hidden layers that split the genotype–anatomy inverse problem
statement: Bioelectric networks mitigate the inverse problem of morphogenesis by acting as 'hidden layers' between genetics and anatomy: the mapping from ion channel genes to bioelectric pattern, and from bioelectric pattern to anatomy, are each easier to invert than the direct genotype–anatomy map, decomposing the control problem into two easier ones for evolution and for engineers.
quote: The relationships of ion channel genes to the bioelectric pattern, and bioelectric pattern to its resulting anatomy, are each easier to invert than the direct genotype–anatomy link, so they help to decompose the control problem into two easier problems.
scope: Bioelectric control of morphogenesis in animals

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Voltage is the instructive variable: an unrelated yeast pump can replace tail V-ATPase
statement: Membrane voltage is a coarse-grained, high-order parameter over ion channel and pump microstates: electrogenic proteins can be swapped as long as the bioelectric state is correct, e.g. the V-ATPase function in tadpole tail regeneration can be phenocopied by a yeast proton pump with no sequence or structural homology.
quote: electrogenic proteins can be swapped out as needed (e.g., V-ATPase complex in the tadpole tail can be phenocopied by a yeast proton pump with no sequence or structural homology, because it produces the correct physiological signal), and everything still works as long as the bioelectric state is correct [190].
scope: Xenopus tadpole tail regeneration; bioelectric control generally

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Genetically wild-type planarian cells can store more than one target morphology
statement: In planaria, a brief (2-day) physiological intervention can reset the bioelectric circuit that controls head number from the default one-head pattern memory to a two-head pattern, so the same genetically wild-type cells can harbour multiple bioelectrically encoded target morphologies that guide regeneration.
quote: In this case, the exact same hardware (genetically wild-type planarian cells) can harbor multiple representations of the bioelectrically encoded target morphology that guides the cellular collectives during regeneration [193–195].
scope: Planarians (Dugesia japonica and related species) during regeneration

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Bioelectric changes let wild-type planaria grow other species' head shapes in days
statement: Head shapes of existing planarian species are readily recapitulated by genetically wild-type planaria whose bioelectric circuit is altered during regeneration, so 100–150 million years of evolutionary distance in morphospace can be crossed in a few days through the dynamics of bioelectric pattern memories.
quote: Indeed, it has been shown that existing planarian species’ head shapes are readily recapitulated by a genetically wild-type animal experiencing changes to its bioelectric circuit during regeneration—100–150 million years of evolutionary distance in morphospace can be crossed in a few days because of the dynamics of bioelectric pattern memories [197, 198].
scope: Planarians (e.g. Girardia dorotocephala) treated with gap-junction blockers during regeneration

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Surgically altered ciliate cortex is inherited across generations despite wild-type DNA
statement: In unicellular ciliates, changes made to cell-surface form can be inherited across generations independently of DNA: surgical rotation of a small patch of cortex creates a stable line in which part of the ciliary beat pushes food out of the mouth, which the wild-type genome cannot correct.
quote: Changes made to unicellular form can persist across generations [203–205]; for example, surgical rotation of a small patch of the cell surface creates a stable line of animals in which a portion of the ciliary beat pushes food out of their mouths—a condition which their perfectly wild-type genome cannot correct.
scope: Ciliates such as Paramecium and Tetrahymena

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Planaria adapt to barium by changing expression of only a handful of genes
statement: Planaria exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker that is evolutionarily novel to them, first lose their heads but then regrow barium-insensitive heads, with only a handful of genes up- or down-regulated, showing that cells can navigate transcriptional space to solve a problem for which there was no selection.
quote: Transcriptional analysis reveals that these tissues up- and down-regulate just a handful of genes to get back to physiological and anatomical setpoints despite the inability to regulate potassium.
scope: Planarians cultured in barium chloride

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Animals with robust regeneration also resist cancer and aging
statement: Animals with robust morphogenetic control due to high plasticity are resistant to perturbation at many scales: they regenerate lost limbs and organs, readily suppress cancer, and resist aging, contrary to the expectation that easy access to undifferentiated cells should make them highly cancer-prone.
quote: Animals with robust morphogenetic control due to high levels of plasticity are resistant to changes of circumstance (injury) at many scales: they regenerate after loss of limbs and organs (degradation of body-scale information), they suppress cancer readily [238] (degradation of tissue-scale information) and they resist aging (degradation of cell-level information).
scope: Animals across taxa, especially highly regenerative ones such as planaria and salamanders

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Competency gains drive a ratchet toward ever greater multiscale competency
statement: Because each gain in developmental competency makes the structural genome harder for selection to evaluate, evolution increasingly optimizes the competency mechanisms themselves, a feedback ratchet for multiscale intelligence that appears in computational models and has run to different extents in planaria, salamanders and mammals.
quote: This starts a feedback loop, because each gain in competency makes it even harder to judge the structural genome, which exacerbates the drive toward improving competencies—a ratchet for multiscale intelligence that can readily be seen in computational models of the process [240].
scope: Evolution of metazoans; computational models of evolving competent cells

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: The competency ratchet predicts no planarian mutant strains with abnormal morphology
statement: The competency-ratchet model predicts, and it is the case, that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (unlike flies or mice), explains the difficulty of making transgenic planaria, and the only known permanent abnormal planarian lines (two-headed and randomized 1- vs 2-head forms) arose from bioelectric rather than genetic change.
quote: For example, it predicts the confirmed fact that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (the way there are for fruit flies, mice, etc.) and explains why the research community has had such a hard time (despite decades of efforts) generating transgenic planaria.
scope: Planarians compared with Drosophila, mice and other model organisms

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Multiscale competency smooths the fitness landscape and lets search escape local maxima
statement: The multiscale competency architecture smooths the fitness landscape by reducing phenotypic differences between genotypes, letting evolution explore mutations that would otherwise be lethal (e.g. a mutation that displaces the mouth but has another benefit survives because the mouth self-corrects), which makes search more efficient and helps it overcome local maxima.
quote: By smoothing the fitness landscape, MCA makes the search process much more efficient, improving evolvability by enabling the search to overcome local maxima.
scope: Evolution of organisms with regulative development

work: Darwin's agential materials: evolutionary implications of multiscale competency in developmental biology
label: Developmental error-correction makes mutations neutral and builds up cryptic variation
statement: By buffering mutational effects through developmental regulation, the multiscale competency architecture makes neutral many mutations that would be deleterious under a direct genotype-to-phenotype mapping, so they persist as a pool of phenotypically dormant cryptic variation that can later be exploited.
quote: MCA makes many mutations neutral that would be deleterious in a direct genotype → phenotype architecture. Such mutations whose effects are mitigated by developmental regulation are not weeded out; instead, they persist, generating over time a rich pool of diversity that may be phenotypically dormant, but can be exploited in future.
scope: Evolving populations of organisms with regulative development

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Physarum learns and decides without neurons, and its behaviour is its morphological change
statement: The unicellular slime mould Physarum learns from repeated experience and makes decisions (e.g. growing towards the heavier of distant inert objects) without a brain, neurons or cellularization, and in Physarum behaviour is implemented as change of body shape, blurring the distinction between morphological and behavioural problems.
quote: These examples of learning and decision-making occur in the absence of a brain, neurons, or cellularization. From the perspective of evolutionary change across behavioral domains, one interesting thing is that for Physarum, its behavior is its morphological change.
scope: Physarum polycephalum (slime mould)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Planarian tail fragments regenerate brains that recall trained behaviour
statement: Tail fragments of planarian flatworms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the trained information, so behavioural memories are apparently imprinted onto the new brain as it forms, linking the information processing that restores body shape with that which preserves past experience.
quote: Tails of worms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the original information: the behavioral memories are apparently also imprinted onto the new brain as it forms (McConnell et al. 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013).
scope: Planarian flatworms (McConnell 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013 with Dugesia japonica)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Xenopus tadpoles with only a tail eye can see through it
statement: Xenopus laevis tadpoles produced with no primary eyes and a single eye on the tail can see out of the ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord, showing that a frog's cellular hardware can adapt within one generation to a radical reconfiguration of its visual system.
quote: Tadpoles of the frog Xenopus laevis can be produced with no primary eyes, but one eye on their tails; these animals can see out of an ectopic eye, which can connect to the spinal cord (Blackiston and Levin 2013).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with transplanted ectopic eyes (author's lab, Blackiston and Levin 2013)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Bioelectric network information cannot be read from transcript or protein levels
statement: Because ion channels open and close post-translationally, the same channels can yield different voltage states depending on cell history and different channels can yield the same voltage map, the information content of a bioelectric network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or proteomic level and must be studied in living tissue.
quote: As a corollary, the information content of this network cannot be read out at the transcriptional or even proteomic level: channels open and close post-translationally, and the same channels can give rise to different voltage states depending on cells’ history, while diverse channels can give rise to the exact same voltage map.
scope: Bioelectric networks of neural and non-neural cells

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Bioelectric networks are a cognitive glue that enlarges the cognitive light cone of cells
statement: Bioelectric networks, through their plasticity, multiscale historicity (memory) and learning capacity, act as a 'cognitive glue' that binds the cybernetic goal-directedness of single cells into a higher-order system pursuing larger-scale goals (a larger cognitive light cone), and this capacity is not unique to brains.
quote: Bioelectric networks, with their inherent plasticity, multiscale historicity, and learning capacity, are an ideal kind of “cognitive glue” that binds the primitive goal-directedness (in the cybernetic sense) of single cells into a higher order system with a larger cognitive light cone (Fig. 1E).
scope: Neural and non-neural cell collectives in multicellular organisms

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Neural bioelectric machinery was an evolutionary pivot from navigating morphospace
statement: Ion channels, gap junctions and neurotransmitters were originally used to control cell behaviours toward morphogenetic outcomes (navigating anatomical morphospace); their use to drive 3D behaviour via muscle is an evolutionary pivot, exapted with a speed-up from hours to milliseconds and a shift from spatial to temporal (spiking) patterns, and this conservation is why neuroscience tools work throughout the body.
quote: The current use of these components to implement behaviors in 3D space by controlling muscle activity represents an evolutionary pivot: their original usage was to navigate anatomical morphospace (Fields et al. 2020) (that is, to control all cell behaviors toward specific morphogenetic outcomes).
scope: Evolution of animal nervous systems from non-neural bioelectric signalling

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Morphogenetic pattern memory habituates: repeatedly amputated axolotl limbs stop regrowing
statement: The anatomical setpoint that guides regeneration is a pattern memory that is stable but modifiable by experience; for example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads the tissue to habituate to the loss and eventually stop trying to regrow.
quote: This pattern memory can, like any good memory, be modified by experience (it is stable, but also labile to the right kinds of stimuli). For example, repeated amputation of axolotl limbs leads to the tissue habituating to the loss of limb and eventually giving up trying to re-grow (Bryant et al. 2017).
scope: Axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) limb regeneration and regenerating animals generally

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Deer antlers re-form an ectopic branch at a past injury site year after year
statement: In deer trophic memory, an ectopic branch is formed in the otherwise stereotyped antler at the location of earlier damage year after year, long after the damaged rack has been shed, a memory of 3D position held by scalp cells that regenerate the antler annually.
quote: Trophic memory in deer (Bubenik and Pavlansky 1965; Lobo et al. 2014) enables an ectopic branch in their otherwise stereotypical antler structure to be formed year after year, at a specific point of earlier damage, long after the damaged antler rack has been shed
scope: Deer (Cervidae) antler regeneration

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Bioelectrically induced two-headed planaria stay two-headed across later regenerations
statement: In planarian flatworms the number of heads a regenerating fragment builds is set by the state of a bioelectric circuit with a default of one; transiently modifying it re-sets it to 'two', and the resulting two-headed worms keep regenerating as two-headed through multiple rounds of cutting without further manipulation, unless the pattern is experimentally reset.
quote: Remarkably, when cut again in multiple subsequent rounds of regeneration (with no further manipulation), the fragments continue to result in two-headed animals. This shift in the target morphology for regeneration is permanent (unless the animal’s bioelectric pattern memory is reset back to a one-headed state by an experimental manipulation).
scope: Planarian flatworms (Dugesia japonica), author's lab (Oviedo et al. 2010; Durant et al. 2019)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Planarian head number is not directly encoded in the genome
statement: How many heads a planarian cellular collective produces is not directly encoded in its genome, since the same wild-type cells can produce 1-, 2- or 0-headed planaria depending on their history; the genome encodes the hardware (e.g. ion channels) while the outcome results from experience-sensitive electrophysiological 'software'.
quote: The question, of how many heads a given cellular collective will produce, is, surprisingly, not directly encoded in its genome because exactly the same, wild-type set of cells can produce 1-, 2-, or 0-headed planaria depending on their history.
scope: Planarian flatworms

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Genetic assimilation of bioelectric phenotypes likely shaped body-plan evolution
statement: Evolutionary changes in ion channel properties that lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes are likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, analogous to the Baldwin effect for learning.
quote: Evolutionary tweaks of ion channel properties that eventually lead to genetic assimilation of bioelectrically induced phenotypes is likely an important aspect of the evolution of body plans and other morphological features, much as the Baldwin effect is thought to be a key dynamic for the role of cognition and learning in evolutionary lineages (Baldwin 1896).
scope: Evolution of animal body plans

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Commensal bacteria can hijack planarian morphogenesis to cause two-headed regeneration
statement: Like parasites that manipulate host neurobehavioural systems, commensal bacteria can override the default planarian morphogenetic control system and cause two-headed regeneration.
quote: the planarian morphogenetic control system too can be hijacked not only by bioengineers (as described above) but also by commensal bacteria which can over-ride the default system and lead to two-headed regeneration (Williams et al. 2020).
scope: Planarian flatworms and their commensal microbiota (Williams et al. 2020)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: A latent two-head bioelectric pattern is a counterfactual memory of the future target form
statement: Because a two-headed bioelectric pattern can exist in an anatomically normal one-headed planarian with normal gene expression, the bioelectric pattern is not a readout of current anatomy but a representation of the target morphology to be built if the animal is injured, in effect a counterfactual memory.
quote: In the case of a two-headed pattern in a one-headed host, this means that the bioelectrical pattern is not a read-out of what the anatomy is currently, but rather a representation of what it should be, weeks later, following regeneration if the animal is injured.
scope: Planarian flatworms with altered bioelectric patterns (Durant et al. 2017)

work: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind
label: Ion channel drugs can make planarian head number flip stochastically at each regeneration
statement: Exposure to ion channel drugs can put the planarian bioelectric circuit into a bistable state in which, at each regeneration, fragments of these 'cryptic' worms randomly regenerate as one-headed or two-headed, analogous to bistability in perceptual systems.
quote: Exposure to ion channel drugs (a physiological experience akin to electrical signals from a retina or other sense organ, not a genetic change) can place the bioelectric circuit into a state in which it cannot decide between two outcomes and flips back and forth stochastically at each regenerative event (recall of target morphology).
scope: Planarian flatworms treated with ion channel or gap-junction drugs (Durant et al. 2017)
